title: 2026 Made Bike Show Favs 02: Bantam, Liminal Machine Works, Mone, Schon, Significant Other, Sklar, Slow Southern Steel, So Far So Good, and Sour – John Watson
content:
Team Radavist is on the ground at the 2026 Made Bike Show, documenting a selection of bikes. During the first day of the show, Spencer, Paul, and John perused the available offerings and selected bikes from Bantam, Liminal Machine Works, Mone, Schon, Significant Other, Sklar, Slow Southern Steel, So Far So Good, and Sour. Read on for a jam-packed gallery full of details on our favs from Day 02!

The Radavist thanks Shimano for sponsoring our Made Bike Show coverage and our independent Reportage!

 

Bantam Bicycles “Big Jim” Single-Speed – John Watson

Portland, Oregon’s Bantam Bicycles delivered the exact bike I wanted to see at the end of my second day shooting at the 2026 Made Bike Show. Amidst all the 32ers and high-tech, Bob Kamzelski kept shit real with the “Big Jim” 27.5-wheeled single-speed cruiser. These bikes are production frames as one of Bob’s “in stock” offerings. For $1,850, you get a frame and fork in a color of your choice.

Keeping the cost lower than a traditional custom Bantam, the Big Jim is built in batches with a stock geometry. Sizing runs from XS to XXXL to fit just about any body. At either end of the Big Jim is a hooded dropout at the fork end and a classic track end at the rear. Blingy da Vinci cranks, with a slender and classic profile, really tie the room together.

Bob’s craft and frame details are sublime, but this stem immediately caught my eye with a big pill window that unveils the handlebar knurling. Bantam hopes to roll out more “in stock” frames including the brand’s most popular model, the Travelall.

Really well done here, Bob. It was a pleasure seeing you!

@BantamBicycles

Liminal Machine Works Tandem – John Watson

Springfield, Oregon-based Liminal Machine Works made a splash last year at Made with a T47 square taper bottom bracket. This year, Brian brought a local client’s tandem in for display. Building a tandem is not exactly daunting for Brian Sorensen, who spent time working for both Co-Motion and Bike Friday. The clients use the bike for overnighters, touring, and around-town riding.

Designing a bicycle for two people comes with several considerations and opportunities for clever design features. Brian used a stoker steerer tube to attach a Paul Boxcar stem as well as a stoker brake lever for an additional Klamper on the rear of the bike.

Perhaps the biggest accomplishment, however, is the complete Cook Brothers Racing tandem crankset. These cranks are notorious for cracking. To use a Gates belt on the non-drive side, prompting Brian to machine a special spider for the CDX belt chainring.

Really good seeing you again, Brian!

@LiminalMachineWorks

Mone Bikes Pre-SB2 – John Watson

Back in 2019, Silver City, New Mexico’s Mone Bikes built a coaster cruiser for a customer. This bike inspired Cjell Mone’s SB2 production model, which launched a few years later. Nicknamed “Juniper,” the client offered to sell the bike back to Cjell for a slight redux. He rebuilt the wheels, using Velocity Dually rims, a Paul front hub, and a Mone coaster cruiser rear hub, and crammed in some 29×3″ Maxxis tires.

The tall headtube badge, truss tri-plane fork, and classic cruiser lines makes this bike a true show stopper.

The finish on Juniper includes some mashing and frame-blueing chevrons, features a Mone “Stupid Slingshot” stem, and uses cranks made from Profile parts. Hidden in the steerer is a knife, made from Silver City juniper wood and a Pakistani Damascus blade. This detail was commonplace in Don McClung’s bike frames. The client wanted a big chainring, 44-tooth, matched with a 28-tooth coaster cooler hub cog.

Always good to see ya, buddy!

@MoneBikes

Schön Studio Lynx Monster Gravel Bike – Paul Kalifatidi

Danielle Schön of Squamish, Canada, brought her multi-year project down to Portland. This bike, dubbed the “Lynx” due to the resemblance to the large pawed feline, was first unveiled at last year’s show… sort of. It caught my eye last year, and the completed version is equally eye catching. This frame is actually the second iteration of the design that Danielle has been working on for Mike Garrigan of CeramicSpeed. Last year’s prototype was more or less a proof of concept for the napkin sketch that Mike gave to Danielle. This was mostly due to the difficulty of modeling the chainstay, tire, and coupler situation. This frame is slated for completion.

From far away, it’s quite difficult to see that this bike does indeed break into two pieces. Danielle spent countless hours creating her own couplers for the chainstays and seatstays. She opted to make her own as there are no couplers that met her aesthetic choice given how slim the stays are. Most couplers are large and made for downtubes and toptubes. Slimmer options exist, but they are cast and weren’t to Danielle’s liking. The result is this wildly capable looking gravel bike that is wildly capable of fitting into a suitcase.

This bike has presence. Perhaps it’s the 2.4″ tires on a gravel bike. Perhaps it’s the crazy unreleased Hunt wheels. Perhaps it’s Danielle’s ability to infuse feline-like capability into a steel form. Perhaps it’s the whole package. Danielle, well done! You know how much I want one.

@SchonStudio

Sklar Bean Bike – Paul Kalifatidi

Yet again, I’m choosing to showcase a bike that isn’t new for this show. This Sklar Bean Bike, owned and frequently operated by Taylor Wallace of Roly Poly Coffee Company, was first exhibited at the inaugural Made in 2023. Back then, it was brand new and had just been built by Adam Sklar for the show. Now, it has four years of beausage of near-daily use in Bozeman, Montana. Zidell Yards is filled with beautiful new bikes, but the ones that have clearly been ridden and loved are the ones I like the most.

I really love this bike. It is quirky and beautiful. It is functional and fun. Clearly, Taylor feels the same. This kind of patina isn’t earned through occasional use, it’s earned through hundreds of bean related rides and even more rides unrelated to the beans. Operating Roly Poly Coffee Company is not easy, but having this bike helps keep the operation rolling.

Taylor might not have his mobile coffee stand to make you a fresh cup of coffee, but he does have the support of Brooks and a Seldom Seen bag filled with beans to hand out. Taylor, thank you, as always, for being here.

@SklarBikes

Slow Southern Steel 32″ Touring Bike – Paul Kalifatidi

Jesse Turner turned up to MADE with a Slow Southern Steel titanium 32″ touring bike that he built for Randy Windle. While this bike might appear quite clean, Randy has already ridden it a few thousand miles. Given it has tour divide-type intentions, this number is going to increase quite a bit. Randy advised Jesse that his brand name might no longer be honest and he might need to consider a rebrand to “Fast Southern Titanium.”

This bike was a stellar example of how many talented makers can mix their skills to create a bike. Jesse made the frame, his first in titanium, and leaned on the expertise of other framebuilders and makers to complete the build. Brian from Rare Earth did the meticulous finish. James of Black Sheep made the fork and handblebars. Brad Bigham made the seatpost. The bags were made by friends at South City Stitchworks. While Jesse might have welded the frame in Fayetteville, Arkansas, it really is an all-over-America made bicycle and a testament to domestic manufacturing.

Jesse, I can only imagine that whatever made Randy laugh like this was as good as your craftsmanship. For a first stab at titanium, this one is a stunner.

@sss.bike

Sour Bicycles Mega Mullet – Spencer Harding

Our first Mega Mullet (32” front, 29” rear) of the show was this Sour Bikes model, featuring a mixed set of Astral wheels. Dripping in White Industries chrome, BTCHN Ti bars, XTR, and Schwalbe Radial tires, this bike looked incredible.

We’re big fans of the Sour here at the Radavist, especially their steel and aluminum full suspension bikes. This bike is a Double Choc with an understroked rear shock, making the bike 120mm/120mm travel when combined with the Manitou 32” fork. This prototype’s pink color was totally eye-watering and almost overloaded my sensor trying to get the color correct.

This prototype is still unridden, but I got to spend some time on a rigid mega mullet setup earlier this year, and I think this could bridge the old and new wheel sizes of the future.

@SourBicycles @AstralCycling

So Far So Good “Dad Bike” – Spencer Harding

Simona was at the show with two very different bikes. One Minvelo cobbled together from donor frames and one bike, very lovingly, built for her father. Her brand, “So Far So Good”, comes from her time guiding tours for Adventure Cycling Association. In a remote stretch of Texas, when spirits got low, a billboard proclaimed, So Far So Good, which very quickly became the motto of their group. I think it’s one of the best bike monikers I’ve heard in a while.

The “Dad Bike” is Simona’s first time fillet brazing, and she was very excited with the results. Her parents have been commuting by bike in NYC for years, and with Simona’s framebuilding skills, she wanted to address some pain points and issues with their current bikes. I hope Simona’s father enjoys the subtle but stunning blue flake of the paint.

I can only imagine the pride of a father getting to ride a bike built by their daughter and, conversely, being able to equip your parent(s) with amazing bikes from your own hands. Well done, Simona…

@SoFarSoGood

Anna Schwinn’s Significant Other Gravel – Spencer Harding

If there ever was a bike ostentatious enough for Anna Schwinn, this Significant Other gravel bike is absolutely dripping in custom anodization- it is (shoutout Ashley Anodizes It)! She got down to the brake adaptors, crank extractor caps, derailleur linkage, hubs, and headset. A few small details from Ogle are mixed in for extra bling. BTCHN bars and seatpost handle the touchpoints on this amazing rig.

Just drool over all the incredible work that went into the details of this bike. Ashley from Significant Other once again knocks it out of the park. But there’s one detail that sticks out and is hard for some people to find…

Anna’s answer to the “Limp Dick Stem” is the “Erect Clit” stem…

@SignificantOther

 

 

Well, that’s a wrap for our second 2026 Made Bike Show gallery. Which bike is your favorite, and what would you like to see us document from the show?
